items.title: I appreciate automated theorem proving probably more than the average person, but the below is ridic...
items.content:
I appreciate automated theorem proving probably more than the average person, but the below is ridiculously ignorant -- pure engagement farming.

Somehow we're supposed to believe that the field of mathematics has made more progress in 2026 than in the 140 years prior... In reality our understanding of mathematics is nearly unchanged compared to 2025, while the 140 prior years saw the development of axiomatic set theory, category theory, algebraic topology, game theory, information theory, chaos theory, all modern statistics, etc...

Math is just night and day if you compare 1880 to 2025. What new insights have we produced in 2026 that exceed that? Ever wonder where those "open problems in math" come from?

items.content:
Added this section from @X's own rules

Most people don't know that AI reply bots are explicitly not permitted to run on here

And duplicate pasting the same reply with automation is the same thing

X has an entire page dedicated to it

The reason for the "Let's connect 🤝" reply spam is simple, people run automated bots (or do it manually) so that when they get a reply with connect in it, they follow the person and that person automatically follows them too

That way they both get 1 new follower, and that brings them closer to the minimum of 500 verified followers to get accepted into X's Monetization program

Before reply spamming paid you good money: about $10 per million views, so they scripted that and auto replied and they made money. But @X killed that in January this year. Now only timeline views pay you money

Also you need 500,000 impressions in the last 3 months (~166,000 per month) to get into X's Monetization Program, so the idea is to pump replies/posts too such a high level that you force these amounts of views

Now the scheme is to grow an account to a few thousand followers, then sell it, or use it for paid product placements, crypto pump and dumps or AI apps/tools

A large part of spam comes from poor countries where just making $100/mo more from X makes a big difference, so I get it, but I think we should also actively fight it because reply spam is destroying this platform and then people will just leave and I don't like that

I made so many friends on here over the last decade and want to continue doing so, if most of my interactions on here are with spam bots, I won't be able to do that anymore!

https://t.co/jDDqmG0c8h

items.content:
Wow! I just used ChatGPT to prove Pythagoras' Theorem! 🤯🤯🤯

Here is the Lean proof:

import Mathlib

theorem pythagoras_rearrangement
    (a b c : ℝ)
    (h_area : (a + b)^2 = 4 * (a * b / 2) + c^2) :
    a^2 + b^2 = c^2 := by
  calc
    a^2 + b^2 =
        (a + b)^2 - 2 * a * b := by ring
    _ = 4 * (a * b / 2) + c^2 - 2 * a * b := by
      rw [h_area]
    _ = c^2 := by ring

items.title: 🧔‍♂️ On Hoodmaps, for some reason the entire city of New York City became tagged green (rich) over t...
items.content:
🧔‍♂️ On Hoodmaps, for some reason the entire city of New York City became tagged green (rich) over time, I thought something was wrong and tried to fix it but was never able to

Hoodmaps works by letting anyone categorize a city's neighborhoods by coloring it based on if it's tourist (red), cool (yellow), rich (green), business (blue), university (dark blue) or crime (dark gray)

It would then take ALL the pixel drawings by everybody over the last decade and calculate the median for every pixel

But it all became "rich", why? So I asked Fable 5.2 today and it figured it out

Over time with more data you get general average tendencies of people that become a problem where big cities are mostly painted rich (green) because people see them as expensive, but that's not very useful information to navigate a city

So Fable 5.2 suggested to calculate each category color by calculating what's more common there than in the city as whole

And it works! And you can see very granular data now like the NYU university area with a spike seeping into Union Square but then being surrounded by tourists, or Hunters Point being a mix of tourists, crime and businesses

Not about a model release but strong applied insight.

Here is my quote from the blog post for the Future of Work Commission that I published a month ago:

"The most dramatic recent development has been in pure mathematics. This year, AI models began solving open problems that had stymied mathematicians for decades. In September, OpenAI published a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, accompanied by a proof formalized in Lean. The Clay Mathematics Institute subsequently said the problem appeared to have been settled, while emphasizing its evaluation process. OpenAI released more than 700 mathematical manuscripts, with results at different stages of verification. The field is being rapidly upended, and how mathematicians adapt may show how other professions will adjust as AI overtakes their work."

https://t.co/MhgTtP5rz1

items.title: One finding in a report by Accenture caught my attention: the main obstacle to AI adoption tends to ...
items.content:
One finding in a report by Accenture caught my attention: the main obstacle to AI adoption tends to change as organizations gain maturity.

I believe this is worth considering when defining an AI roadmap, because priorities may change as adoption expands. 

Microblog @antgrasso

The research draws on a survey of 510 executives in the UK and Ireland. Among organizations still experimenting with AI, workforce readiness is the most common constraint.

When adoption extends across teams, the digital core tends to become the limiting factor. People may have learned to use AI, but the technology needs to work with the data and systems that support business operations.

For organizations already using AI in their core operations, the challenge shifts toward strategy. Where should the next investment go, and how should the company coordinate its AI initiatives?

I believe this finding is worth considering when defining an AI roadmap, because what worked during experimentation may need to change as adoption expands.

Of course, a shift in the main bottleneck does not mean the previous problems have disappeared. People still need to develop their skills as AI changes their work.

The investment that helped you reach your current level of maturity may not be the one that takes you to the next.

#AIStrategy #DigitalTransformation

Cars kill 1.2 million people every year, yet we don't c...
items.content:
All technologies have upside and downside. 

Cars kill 1.2 million people every year, yet we don't care about that. There's such an optimistic side that the AI safety researchers aren't looking at yet:
• Our food is going to get better with robots.
• Our health is going to get better with sensors on our skin.
• Our transportation is getting better due to automation.
• Our factories are getting better due to automation.

Retail, and every business, gets better when it's automated. 

Aside: Do you want the smartest model running your society or the dumbest?

Smarter intelligence lead to a much better world, as long as we keep the negatives from happening.

When databases came out, the Nazis used that in the Holocaust. Did we stop using databases? No, because they have a huge good to society. 

We don't look at just the costs of something; if we did, we wouldn't drive.

We look at what it can do for us: AI can do everything from build you a video game to build you a new kind of drug, and a whole lot more.

Soon we're going to give robots the ability to move around the real world, image it, understand it, and manipulate it. This could lead to a societal overthrow if we do it improperly. But if done properly, it leads to goodness for all of us.

So let's do it properly.

Remember, if you're scared, the AI safety people get a raise.

When I was 17 I saw HP automate what mom 30 minutes to do and did it in 20 seconds with a machine.

I have always known automation is coming for people who can’t change.

It will help. @boardyai helps me.

items.content:
I hope this gets fixed, and I feel really bad for those people. I'd be pissed if it were me, for sure.

Here is what I'm currently doing:

1. I'm processing every reply I get to flag bots.

2. I have a very high threshold for marking a reply as an AI reply. If there's not enough evidence, I don't assume it's AI.

3. When one account has replied 10 times to me and all of those 10 are AI replies, I block and report you.

So, to get blocked, you are either:

A) Extremely unlucky

B) A bot who replied using AI 10 times in a short period to my account.

I've been doing this for a month now, and my replies are 500% better. I can finally see replies like yours and answer back!

So, there's something else I need to decide:

1. Do I only block people who reply to my account?

2. Or, do I also contribute those bots to a broader list where that will help other people?

I decided to contribute.

I'd love for X to have an official mechanism to report and block these bots, but they don't, so the next best thing is what @levelsio built.

No, it's not perfect, but I know he cares as much as I do to make this work for the good of the platform. I want him to succeed because it's good for me, for you, and for everyone else here.

So, while I hate that there are false positives on that list and I'll do whatever I can to avoid those, I don't see any other good alternatives to clean this place until X decides to act.

I'm happy to hear any different ideas. I'm just not willing to do nothing.

What a special evening sharing the stage with two amazing women: @wenschmidt and Sally Kornbluth from @MIT. We got to have nuanced conversations around AI and its impact on interdisciplinary science. 

At @Caltech we have been advanced AI+Science for more than a decade before it become mainstream. Building interdisciplinarity into the DNA of every university is essential in this age of AI disruption. The projects we are working on to understand and simulate physics at all scales are helping us design better medical catheters, drugs, nuclear fusion reactors, quantum devices that can have widespread benefits. Building physical AI models that are not just LLMs allows us to touch all these areas and open new opportunities for invention and discovery. @schmidtsciences

@liquidai has released d1.3-ultra, updating their d1.2-ultra flagship decision model.

Key results:

➤ d1.3-ultra scores 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. d1.3-ultra achieves the same score as Bison 31B and is a 1-point improvement over d1.2-ultra

➤ d1.3-ultra sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. d1.3-ultra costs $133 per one million Artificial Analysis Decision Index tasks and sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier

Additional model details:

➤ Context window: 64K tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.042 per 1M input tokens, with no charge for output

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input

➤ Providers: Available through Liquid AI’s first-party API

To address this, we can convert our estimated ECI to, for example, the 50% time horizon from @METR_Evals, as the ECI and (the log of) the time horizon are very strongly positively correlated.

Using the updated time-horizon estimates from METR’s Nov 20 report results in the graph below.

Anthropic's lead is 1.4–4.6 ECI points in 2026. In time-horizon terms, it grows from ~4 hours (February) to ~35 hours (late September), mainly because each ECI point adds more hours (in absolute terms) as models improve.

items.title: This, of course, relies on an extrapolation: Anthropic’s best internal models are up to ~1 doubling ...
items.content:
This, of course, relies on an extrapolation: Anthropic’s best internal models are up to ~1 doubling beyond the top model METR measured. However, the simple rule of thumb (~5 ECI points per doubling in the 50% METR time horizon) appears to work surprisingly well over multiple orders of magnitude in task length, from ~7 minutes (GPT-4o) to ~40 hours (GPT-6 Astra).

Other caveats: METR’s time horizons for the top models are very uncertain, and the ECI values of Anthropic’s internal models are themselves estimates, based on Anthropic’s internal version of the ECI (the AECI), as reported in the Nov 5 report by @METR_Evals. Finally, AI companies may spend much more on inference internally than external users can, which could further widen the gap.
items.author: @Research_FRI
items.summary: Research_FRI details caveats to their Anthropic lead estimate: internal models sit ~1 doubling beyond what METR measured, a rule of thumb of ~5 ECI points per doubling of 50% task time horizon holds from GPT-4o (~7 min) to GPT-6 Astra (~40 hours), and METR/ECI values for internal models are themselves estimates, with possible additional inference-spend advantages.

items.title: Here is the 10,000 ft big picture perspective on what I had set out to do. Most programs of unifying...
items.content: Here is the 10,000 ft big picture perspective on what I had set out to do. Most programs of unifying General Relativity (GR) with the Standard Model (SM) set out from the perspective that *geometry* is fundamental, GR is a theory of geometrodynamics, so let's try to make SM another gemetrodynamic theory. My thesis has been that SM is actually fundamental, that it's essentially a theory of transformations of *fields* which are object in a Hilbert space of functions, so how about we try to *field theorize* GR instead.

> 1. Section II.B.2, "Posting automated mentions and replies" (the main one)
> Mass unsolicited auto-replies get labelled an "abuse of the feature, and is not permitted."
> Keyword-search-triggered auto-replies are the example X gives of what's banned, and replying to every post is broader than that. 
> Your bot would fail all four conditions for an allowed auto-reply: prior opt-in from the recipient (they replied to you or messaged you), a simple opt-out you act on quickly, a single automated reply per interaction, and the reply landing on that user's own original post. 
> 
> 2. Section I.A, "Multiple posts/accounts" and "Spamming"
> Identical or near-identical posts from one account are off-limits here, which covers "happy to connect" repeated every minute.

AI Agents & Harnesses Foundations — Building from ReAct Loops to Agent Harnesses with Harness Engineering, LangChain, and LangGraph: https://t.co/cmja8xiLk5 from @PacktPublishing 

“Harness design is key to performance at the frontier of agentic coding.” — Anthropic Engineering, 2026

Amazon Summary: 
"Go beyond simple prompts and build production-grade AI agents with LangChain and LangGraph, from ReAct reasoning loops to tool-calling and context engineering. This book shows you how to build the AI agents and agent harnesses powering modern agentic AI applications. You'll start with LangChain's core primitives, including models, messages, prompts, tools, and structured outputs, and use them to build increasingly capable agents. From there, you'll go under the hood to understand the agent loop, tool-calling LLMs, state, memory, context engineering, orchestration, and long-horizon agents. Using LangChain, LangGraph, and LangSmith, you'll see how modern agent systems are built, orchestrated, traced, and observed. By the end, you'll understand modern agent harness architecture and have the practical foundations to build, debug, secure, and evolve reliable production AI agents."

items.title: @TrishaCode I have studied resisters every time there is a paradigm shift, and they are always there...
items.content:
@TrishaCode I have studied resisters every time there is a paradigm shift, and they are always there. It bugged me so much for decades that I studied them and did a lot of consumer research around America, which is what led to eight books about the future that were pretty accurate (if you listen to the Amazon reviews, which are accurate; I didn't influence them). 

People think that what they learn to do is creative. It is creative while you're learning, but once you're doing, it's not really that creative.

items.content:
Daily Sedecordle 

Sedecordle is a fun challenge, but there’s no established evidence that playing it raises IQ, improves everyday memory, or lowers your risk of Alzheimer’s. Solving all 16 words is impressive. It tells you how you did on the puzzle. 

A 78-week trial of 107 adults with mild cognitive impairment found that crossword puzzles modestly outperformed computer games on a cognitive test. The trial didn’t test Sedecordle or establish that word puzzles prevent Alzheimer’s. (Devanand et al., 2022) 

The following sources cover brain training, working memory, crosswords, and dementia risk. The crossword trial found a modest cognitive test benefit in adults with mild cognitive impairment, and the WHO rated the evidence for cognitive stimulation to reduce cognitive decline or dementia risk as very low certainty but never actually ruled out prevention of Alzheimer's. Sedecordle itself was outside the scope of these studies.

items.content:
Street Glide - 121 Cubic Inch Engine! 

Harley-Davidson - Nearly 1000 Lb!

The challenge begins before you even hit the street. Imagine backing a nearly 1,000 lb Harley-Davidson out of your garage, sitting astride the motorcycle, using nothing but your feet to push it backward while simultaneously maintaining its balance. Even a slight driveway incline, uneven concrete surface, or unexpected lean can make this seemingly simple maneuver physically demanding.

A nearly 1000 lb Harley-Davidson is challenging to maneuver at low speeds, particularly for beginners.

Unlike highway cruising, where the motorcycle benefits from dynamic stability, garage maneuvering occurs at virtually zero velocity right out of the door. The rider must manage the enormous gravitational torque, center of gravity, and lateral equilibrium without the stabilizing effects of forward motion.

The complexities of riding a heavyweight motorcycle on the street go far beyond its massive engine displacement and raw power.

All New Harley!
